These surge-type glaciers flow slowly for decades and then, over months or a few years, speed up to ten or even a hundred times their usual rate. In 1953 the Kutiah Glacier in what is now Pakistan reportedly advanced about 12 kilometers in roughly three months. Such glaciers are not spread evenly across the world but cluster in a few regions, including Alaska, Svalbard, and the Karakoram mountains.

The best-documented surge took place at Variegated Glacier in Alaska, which had surged roughly every twenty years. Expecting another event, a team that included the glaciologist Barclay Kamb monitored the glacier for years beforehand. When it surged in 1982 and 1983, they found that water pressure at its base had risen sharply. Normally, meltwater drains away through a few large tunnels in the ice. During the surge, the researchers concluded, this system had been replaced by a network of many small, linked cavities that held the water back, so the ice was partly lifted off its bed and slid rapidly.

The surge ended suddenly in early July 1983, when a large flood of muddy water burst from the glacier's front and the ice slowed within days. Not every surge fits this pattern, however. Glaciers in Svalbard tend to surge more slowly and for longer, and other causes have been proposed for them.

Many dung beetles in Africa do not eat their food where they find it. Instead, a beetle shapes a piece of dung into a ball and rolls it away, pushing backward with its hind legs, head down. Speed matters, because other beetles at the dung pile may try to steal a finished ball, and a straight line carries a beetle away from the pile faster than a winding path would. Before setting off, a beetle often climbs onto its ball and turns around on top of it, a movement that researchers believe helps it read the sky.

By day, beetles can steer by the Sun, and earlier research had shown that some species can use the pattern of polarized light around the Moon. In 2013, however, a team led by Marie Dacke reported that the South African species Scarabaeus satyrus kept a straight course even on moonless nights. When the researchers fitted beetles with small cardboard caps that blocked their view of the sky, the insects wandered in loops. Tested in a planetarium in Johannesburg, the beetles rolled fairly straight when only the band of the Milky Way was displayed, which suggests that they orient by its broad stripe of light rather than by individual stars.

It was reportedly the first known case of an animal using the Milky Way to orient. Birds, seals, and humans can steer by stars, but a beetle's small eyes probably cannot resolve most of them, so a bright band may serve in their place.

Economists in the 1940s often described the economy as a circular flow: households spend money on goods, the money becomes firms' revenue, and firms pay it back out as wages. In 1949 Bill Phillips, a New Zealand-born engineer who had turned to economics as a student at the London School of Economics, took the metaphor literally. He is said to have built a machine of tanks, pipes, and valves in a garage, in which colored water stood for money moving through a national economy.

The machine, later known as MONIAC, stood about two meters tall. Water was pumped to the top to represent national income and then flowed downward, some of it diverted into tanks for taxes, savings, and spending on imports, while the rest continued to circulate. Turning a valve representing a tax rate changed the water levels throughout the system, and because water takes time to move, students could watch the effects of a policy spread gradually rather than appear all at once. The machine also solved, in effect, a set of equations that most students of the time could not have solved on paper.

Phillips demonstrated it at a seminar at his school, and roughly a dozen copies were eventually built for universities and other buyers, reportedly including a central bank and a car company. Phillips himself became far better known for a 1958 paper relating unemployment to the rate at which wages rose. Several of his machines survive in museums.

When the archaeologist Arthur Evans excavated the palace of Knossos on Crete after 1900, he found thousands of clay tablets inscribed in a script he called Linear B. Its signs fell into two kinds: small pictures, such as a horse or a three-legged pot, that stood for whole words, and about ninety other signs used to spell words out. That number was a clue. An alphabet typically needs only twenty to thirty letters, while a script with a sign for every word needs thousands, so a set of about ninety suggested a syllabary, in which each sign stands for a syllable such as ka or to.

In the 1940s the American classicist Alice Kober noticed that certain words appeared in groups that shared a beginning but had different endings, as forms of one word do in languages such as Latin. Building on her work, the British architect Michael Ventris arranged the signs in a grid, grouping those that seemed to share a consonant or a vowel before knowing any sounds. When a large whale dies in the open ocean, its body often sinks to the sea floor, where it can become one of the richest sources of food in an otherwise sparse environment. Most of the deep sea receives only a thin drizzle of organic particles drifting down from the surface. A carcass weighing forty tons can therefore deliver, in a single event, roughly as much food as the same patch of mud might otherwise collect over centuries. Scientists first came across such a "whale fall" by chance in 1987, when a research submarine off southern California passed over a skeleton surrounded by bacterial mats and clams.

Studies of natural and deliberately sunk carcasses suggest that a whale fall passes through overlapping stages. First, mobile scavengers such as hagfish and sleeper sharks strip away the soft tissue, which can take from months to a couple of years. Finally, bacteria slowly break down the oils stored inside the bones, releasing hydrogen sulfide that feeds other microbes, and this stage may last for decades.

In late autumn and early winter, towns along the eastern and southern shores of the Great Lakes can be buried by snow while places a few dozen kilometers away stay clear. This pattern, known as lake-effect snow, begins when cold air, often arriving from Canada behind a passing storm, crosses a lake whose water is still relatively warm. The lake warms the lowest layer of air and adds moisture through evaporation. Because the warmed air is lighter than the colder air above it, it rises and cools as it rises, so its moisture condenses into clouds that can drop heavy snow over land.

Several factors control how much snow falls. One is the difference in temperature between the lake surface and the air about 1.5 kilometers up; forecasters often look for a difference of roughly 13 degrees Celsius or more. Another is fetch, the distance the wind travels over open water. Wind blowing along the length of a long, narrow lake such as Lake Ontario gathers far more moisture than wind crossing it the short way, and it can produce narrow bands of intense snow. Hills near the shore add to the effect by forcing the air to rise farther.

The effect usually weakens later in winter, as the water cools, and on lakes that freeze over, ice cuts off much of the supply of heat and moisture. Lake Erie, the shallowest of the Great Lakes, freezes over most often, which is one reason its season tends to end earlier.

In late autumn and early winter, towns along the eastern and southern shores of the Great Lakes can be buried by snow while places a few dozen kilometers away stay clear. This pattern, known as lake-effect snow, begins when cold air, often arriving from Canada behind a passing storm, crosses a lake whose water is still relatively warm. Because the warmed air is lighter than the colder air above it, it rises and cools as it rises, so its moisture condenses into clouds that can drop heavy snow over land.

In the early eighteenth century, the German chemist Georg Ernst Stahl, building on ideas of Johann Joachim Becher, proposed that every material able to burn contained a substance he called phlogiston. When wood burned, the theory held, it released its phlogiston into the air and left ash behind. Metals were treated the same way: heating a metal in air turned it into a powder called a calx, which was explained as the metal minus its phlogiston. The theory also seemed to explain why a flame in a sealed jar soon went out, since the air could absorb only a limited amount of phlogiston.

The idea organized chemical thinking for decades, but it faced a stubborn problem. Careful workers had found that a metal's calx weighed more than the metal it came from, which was strange if something had been lost. Some supporters suggested that phlogiston might have negative weight, or that it made substances lighter in some other way, but these proposals satisfied few chemists.

In the 1770s the French chemist Antoine Lavoisier attacked the problem by weighing substances carefully in closed vessels. He concluded that burning and the formation of a calx involved combining with part of the air rather than giving something off, and he named that part oxygen. Ironically, the English chemist Joseph Priestley, who had isolated the same gas in 1774, called it "dephlogisticated air" and defended the phlogiston theory until his death in 1804. By then, however, most chemists had accepted Lavoisier's account.

Around their first birthday, most infants who see themselves in a mirror react as if they were looking at another child. They smile at the image, reach toward it, or look behind the glass. In 1972 the psychologist Beulah Amsterdam reported a simple test of when children recognize the reflection as themselves, adapting a method used earlier with chimpanzees. A mother secretly dabbed a spot of rouge on her child's nose and then placed the child in front of a mirror. A child who touched his or her own nose, not the one in the mirror, was taken to recognize the self.

In Amsterdam's study and many later ones, few children younger than about fifteen months passed, while a majority did so by about age two. Researchers have linked this change to others that appear around the same time, such as using one's own name and showing embarrassment, and some have argued that the test marks the beginning of a concept of self.

Later work has questioned how widely the test applies. A study published in 2011 reported that very few children aged about one and a half to six in rural Kenya removed the mark, although many of them stared closely at their reflection. The authors suggested that the children may have recognized themselves but did not treat a strange mark on their face as something to remove, perhaps because of local expectations about behaving with unfamiliar adults. If so, failing the test does not always show a lack of self-recognition.

Around their first birthday, most infants who see themselves in a mirror react as if they were looking at another child. They smile at the image, reach toward it, or look behind the glass. In 1972 the psychologist Beulah Amsterdam reported a simple test of when children recognize the reflection as themselves, adapting a method used earlier with chimpanzees. A mother secretly dabbed a spot of rouge on her child's nose and then placed the child in front of a mirror. A child who touched his or her own nose, not the one in the mirror, was taken to recognize the self.

In Amsterdam's study and many later ones, few children younger than about fifteen months passed, while a majority did so by about age two. Researchers have linked this change to others that appear around the same time, such as using one's own name and showing embarrassment, and some have argued that the test marks the beginning of a concept of self.

Later work has questioned how widely the test applies. A study published in 2011 reported that very few children aged about one and a half to six in rural Kenya removed the mark, although many of them stared closely at their reflection. The authors suggested that the children may have recognized themselves but did not treat a strange mark on their face as something to remove, perhaps because of local expectations about behaving with unfamiliar adults. If so, failing the test does not always show a lack of self-recognition.

The Pantheon in Rome, rebuilt under the emperor Hadrian and completed around 125 CE, is roofed by a concrete dome about 43 meters across. It is still the largest dome of unreinforced concrete in the world. Roman builders made concrete from lime, water, and a volcanic ash now called pozzolana, after the town of Pozzuoli near Naples, combined with chunks of stone or broken brick. The ash reacted with the lime to form a material that hardened even in damp conditions.

The size of the dome posed a problem, because concrete resists crushing far better than it resists being pulled apart. A heavy dome tends to spread outward near its base, and if the lower parts crack, the structure can fail. The builders reduced the load in several ways. They graded the stone mixed into the concrete, using heavy material near the base and progressively lighter material higher up, ending with pumice, a light volcanic rock, near the top. They also set rows of sunken square panels, called coffers, into the inner surface, removing weight while leaving ribs of concrete between them. At the crown, a round opening about eight meters wide, the oculus, removes the top of the dome entirely and lets in light.

The walls that carry the dome are about six meters thick, and studies suggest that heavy rings of masonry stepped around the lower dome help hold it in place. Cracks have appeared over the centuries, but the dome continues to stand.

Most people can tell whether one note is higher than another, and many can sing a familiar tune starting from any note. Far fewer have absolute pitch, often called perfect pitch: the ability to name or sing a particular note, such as C sharp, without first hearing a reference note. A frequently quoted estimate is that about one person in ten thousand in Western countries has the ability, though the figure is hard to measure and may be too low.

Two findings suggest that experience plays a large part. First, people with absolute pitch usually began musical training early, often before about the age of six, and the ability is rare among those who started later. This has led researchers to propose a sensitive period in childhood for linking pitches to names. Second, the psychologist Diana Deutsch and her colleagues reported that conservatory students in Beijing were far more likely to have absolute pitch than U.S. conservatory students who had begun training at the same ages. Deutsch suggested that speaking Mandarin, a tone language in which the pitch of a syllable can change its meaning, may make it easier to attach labels to pitches early in life.

A third line of research suggests that memory for pitch is more widespread than the ability to name notes. In a 1994 study, Daniel Levitin asked ordinary people to sing popular songs they knew from recordings. Many came within about two semitones of the recorded key, evidently remembering a pitch that they could not name.
